q: American labels once carried the words Chablis, Burgundy and Champagne on wine grown nowhere near any of those places. What closed the practice to new brands?
opts: A Supreme Court ruling on consumer deception
The registration of those names as American trademarks
A 2006 trade agreement between the United States and the European Union
A federal statute banning all foreign place names on domestic wine
exp: Brands already using the terms were allowed to continue, which is why a small number of such labels survive on shelves. Grandfather the old and close the door on the new is the standard settlement when a long-established brand collides with a protected indication.

q: A European appellation wants its name defended in a country that keeps no register of geographical indications at all. What is the usual route?
opts: A bilateral agreement, or registering the name as a certification mark
The name is automatically protected everywhere once registered at home
Nothing can be done until that country builds a register
The World Trade Organization enforces the name directly on request
exp: Protection is territorial, so a name vigorously defended at home may be free for anyone to use a border away until something is signed or filed. It is why certain famous European names exist as appellations in one country and as collective or certification marks in another, doing the same job through different machinery.

q: Appellations outside Europe were mostly drawn as boundaries first, with production rules arriving late or never at all. Which explanation is usually given?
opts: European law forbade them from adopting production rules of their own
Their climates are so reliable that production rules would serve no purpose
Their governments lacked the constitutional power to regulate farming
Those regions were planted by growers free to choose variety and method
exp: A European appellation codifies what growers were already doing, and a region with no settled practice gives a rulebook nothing to write down; a newer scheme records instead where growers turned out to be doing well. That difference in order, rather than any difference in seriousness, is the honest account of why one kind of system dictates the grape and the other does not.

q: Nothing in the glass or in the laboratory proves with certainty which vineyard a wine came from. What does that force every origin scheme in the world to rest on?
opts: The word of the producer, backed by nothing
A panel of tasters familiar with the region
Audited records following the fruit from the vineyard through the cellar to the bottle
Chemical fingerprinting of the finished wine, which can place any bottle in its own vineyard
exp: Isotope and trace-element work can corroborate a claim, but it cannot originate one, so paperwork carries the whole weight of origin law. That is also why wine fraud is overwhelmingly a documents crime rather than a cellar one, and why inspectors spend their days in offices.

q: A dismal vintage in a famous appellation still produces bottles carrying the full appellation name. Why does the law allow that?
opts: The appellation is suspended automatically in years officially rated poor
Members vote each year on whether the name may be used
The name may be used only once a vintage rating has been published
Compliance is tested wine by wine, and the year itself is not a legal question
exp: A rulebook can ask whether this wine met the requirements and cannot ask whether the season was any good. Producers answer the gap themselves by declassifying weak lots, and the buyer answers it by knowing the year, which is why vintage knowledge survives in an age of technical competence.

q: Alongside origin law, a second and entirely separate body of law governs wine almost everywhere and has nothing to do with where it grew. Which?
opts: The safety rules covering machinery in the cellar
Excise duty and the licensing of the wine trade
The ranking of a region's vineyards into crus
The authorisations that cap new vineyard planting
exp: Duty is charged by volume and often by strength, which is why bottle sizes, strength statements and cellar registers interest revenue authorities as much as wine bodies. A sommelier meets this body of law every working night, in service hours, in age checks and in the terms of the premises licence.

q: Until 2012 a European bottle could claim only to be made from organically grown grapes, never to be organic wine. What did the regulation of that year add?
opts: Rules governing the cellar as well as the vineyard, including a lower ceiling on sulphur dioxide
A prohibition on all added sulphur dioxide
A requirement that the wine be sold unfiltered, so that nothing is stripped out after fermentation
A ban on exporting organic wine outside the union
exp: Certification had stopped at the winery door, so nothing in law said what could be done to the fruit once it arrived. Fixing permitted cellar practices completed the claim and turned a farming certificate into a description of the wine itself.

q: A merchant leaves a case of classified wine beside a radiator for a summer and pours it, cooked, to a guest. What does the appellation's rulebook say about that?
opts: The producer must replace any bottle spoiled in storage
Storage temperature is fixed by the rulebook all the way down to the glass
The name is forfeited automatically as soon as a bottle is found in poor condition
Nothing at all, since its requirements are spent once the wine has left the producer
exp: A wine that satisfied every requirement in the vineyard and the cellar can still be destroyed in a hot warehouse or a sunlit window, and no origin law reaches that far. Everything after the sale is left to trade practice and to ordinary consumer law, which is why a merchant's and a sommelier's own handling matters more to what the guest tastes than any letters on the label do.

q: Inspections, laboratory work and the administration behind a European denomination all cost money. Who pays for them?
opts: General taxation in the member state, since the controls serve the public
The buyer, through a surcharge collected at retail
The producers, through levies on their wine
The European Commission, from a central fund
exp: A denomination is largely self-financing, which gives its members a direct interest in how thoroughly it is policed and in who else is admitted to use the name. It also explains why a small appellation with few producers struggles to fund the controls a large one takes for granted.

q: A rotating perforated drum with paddles inside throws bunches against its wall, the berries drop through the holes and the woody frames travel out of the far end. Which cellar operation is that machine performing?
opts: Pressing
Destemming
Fining
Racking
exp: Taking the stalks off removes a green, bitter element and hands the winemaker the decision of how much stem character the wine gets, rather than accepting whatever the bunch happened to bring. Crushing is a separate action entirely, and a good machine can strip every stem without breaking a single berry.

q: Crushed black grapes are held at eight degrees for four days and the yeast are kept from starting. What is chiefly being drawn out of the skins in that window?
opts: Tannin and structure, with little colour
Colour and aroma, with little tannin
Sugar out of the pulp inside the berry
Sharp acidity out of the seeds
exp: Grape pigment dissolves readily in water while tannin needs alcohol to come out in quantity, so a cold soak loads colour and fruit aroma without hardening the wine. There is no alcohol in the vat yet to defend it, which is why the step is run cold and under a protective gas.

q: Bunches travel along a vibrating belt where hands pull out shrivelled berries, leaves and anything mouldy before the crusher. Which flaw is that work preventing, given that nothing later in the cellar removes it cleanly?
opts: Cloudiness in the young wine, which no filter fully clears
A protein haze appearing in warm weather
Green and mouldy flavours carried in on the fruit
Tartrate crystals dropping out in the bottle later
exp: A sorting table is the cheapest quality tool in the building because taint travels forward: a single handful of mouldy fruit marks a whole vat, and the treatments that chase the flavour back out strip the wine's own fruit along with it. Optical sorters do the same job by camera and air jet, fast enough to keep up with a machine harvest.

q: A white must sits stubbornly cloudy for two days, so the winemaker doses it with a preparation that breaks down the gum holding the fine particles in suspension. What has been added?
opts: A pectolytic enzyme
Extra sulphur dioxide
A cultured yeast
Tartaric acid
exp: Pectin is a natural gum in the grape that keeps solids afloat, and the enzyme cuts it so they fall within hours instead of days. The same preparations are used to raise the yield at the press and to help colour come out of red skins.

q: A cellar hand stands on a plank above an open wooden vat and pushes the floating raft of skins under with a wooden plunger. Which French term names that?
opts: Foulage
Remontage
Remuage
Pigeage
exp: Working by hand or by foot gives a soft, unhurried extraction, and the operator can feel how much the cap will give up, which is why it survives in cellars making delicate reds. The drawbacks are heat, the carbon dioxide sitting over the vat and the labour of repeating it three times a day.

q: Wine is drawn from a valve at the base of a red fermenter and sprayed back over the skins through a hose. Beyond wetting the cap, what does that circulation supply?
opts: A measured dose of oxygen for the yeast
Sugar to restart a ferment that has slowed
A steady fall in the wine's alcohol
The carbon dioxide that protects the vat
exp: Yeast need a little oxygen early on to build healthy cell membranes and carry the sugar all the way down, and splashing wine through air is how a red ferment gets it. The operation is remontage, and how hard and how often it is run is one of the main levers on how much a red extracts.

q: The entire contents of a fermenting red tank are run into an empty vessel, the cap left to drain onto the screen, and the wine then returned over the top of it. What does that achieve which a straightforward pump-over does not?
opts: The seeds settle out and can be left behind, taking their tannin with them
It flushes the tank with carbon dioxide, so the cap is shielded from air
It raises the alcohol, since part of the wine evaporates in the transfer
It halts the ferment for a day, since the wine stands in an empty tank
exp: Delestage, or rack and return, also breaks the cap apart completely and aerates hard, so it is an aggressive tool rather than a gentle one. Leaving the seeds on the floor of the vessel is the point of it, since far less of their hard tannin then reaches the wine. Cellars reach for it early, when they want extraction and a clean tannin profile, and stop before the wine is stripped.
